knownFor.label: Golestan Palace
knownFor.note: The Qajar royal palace in Tehran, a UNESCO site.

location.value: Iran, ruled from Tehran. It lost the South Caucasus to Russia in the early 19th century.

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau, mountains and deserts, plus the Caspian and Persian Gulf coasts.
terrain.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

climate.value: Arid and semi-arid. The Great Persian Famine of 1870–72.
climate.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

resources.value: Agriculture and carpets, then oil (discovered in 1908) dominating the 20th-century economy.
resources.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

disasters.value: Famines (1870–72, and during the First World War occupation) and earthquakes.
disasters.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

population.value: About 9 million around 1812. 33,708,744 in the 1976 census (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Tehran grew from the Qajar capital into a large modern city under the Pahlavis.
urbanisation.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

disease.value: Cholera and plague epidemics in the 19th century.
disease.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

migration.value: Rural-to-urban migration in the 1960s–70s after land reform.
migration.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

economicBase.value: Agriculture and crafts under the Qajars. Oil revenue and state-led industrialisation under the Pahlavis.
economicBase.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

tradeRoutes.value: Foreign concessions (e.g. the 1872 Reuters concession, cancelled) and the Anglo-Persian Oil Company (from 1909). Mosaddegh nationalised the oil industry in 1951.

wealth.value: GDP about $77.99 billion nominal ($2,101 per person) in 1978 (Wikipedia infobox estimate).

moneyAndTax.value: The toman and qiran (Qajar), then the rial (Pahlavi). Oil revenues fell sharply in 1977.

inequality.value: Landlords, tribes and clergy dominated under the Qajars. The White Revolution (1963) brought land reform, but development was uneven.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy (Qajar), then a constitutional monarchy after 1906. The Pahlavi state was a semi-constitutional monarchy, increasingly autocratic, with one-party rule from 1975.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Qajar Iran (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox); Wikipedia: Pahlavi Iran (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox)

keyRulers.value: Agha Mohammad Khan (1789–1797, founder). Fath-Ali Shah. Naser al-Din Shah (1848–1896). Reza Shah Pahlavi (1925–1941). Mohammad Reza Shah (1941–1979).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Qajar dynasty, until parliament deposed it (1925) in favour of Reza Khan, founder of the Pahlavi dynasty.

institutions.value: The Majlis (parliament) after the Constitutional Revolution (1906). Amir Kabir’s reforms (the Dar al-Funun school, 1851). Pahlavi centralisation and secularisation.

stability.value: The Constitutional Revolution (1905–11), the 1921 coup, the 1953 coup against Mosaddegh (backed by the US and Britain), and the 1978–79 revolution.

eliteConflict.value: Shahs versus clergy and the merchant bazaar, and later versus nationalists and the left. The SAVAK secret police repressed opposition.

armyAndTech.value: Weak armies under the Qajars (the Persian Cossack Brigade, 1879). A large, modern, US-equipped army under Mohammad Reza Shah.
armyAndTech.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

majorWars.value: Russo-Persian Wars (1804–13, 1826–28; the treaties of Gulistan and Turkmenchay). The Herat wars. Occupation in both World Wars (Anglo-Soviet invasion, 1941).

territoryChange.value: Lost the Caucasus to Russia (1813, 1828) and Herat (1857). About 1,648,195 km² under the Pahlavis.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Qajar Iran (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox); Wikipedia: Pahlavi Iran (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox)

alliancesRivals.value: Pressure from Russia and Britain, which divided it into spheres in 1907. A US ally under Mohammad Reza Shah.

inventions.value: Railways (the Trans-Iranian Railway, 1938), modern industry and the oil industry under the Pahlavis.
inventions.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

scienceEducation.value: The Dar al-Funun (1851), the University of Tehran (1934), and mass education in the White Revolution.
scienceEducation.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

openness.value: Westernising modernisation under both Pahlavi shahs, which provoked religious and nationalist opposition.

communicationTransport.value: Caravans and caravanserais; the telegraph (1860s); the Trans-Iranian Railway (1938).

religion.value: Twelver Shiʿa Islam, with Sunni, Jewish, Zoroastrian, Christian and Baháʼí minorities.

languageWriting.value: Persian (Azerbaijani Turkish at the Qajar court).

artsArchitecture.value: Qajar portrait painting and the Golestan Palace. Pahlavi modernist architecture (the Azadi Tower, 1971).
artsArchitecture.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

socialStructure.value: Shah and court, landlords and tribal chiefs, clergy, merchants and peasants. A new urban middle class under the Pahlavis.
socialStructure.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

sharedIdentity.value: Persian and Shiʿa identity. Pahlavi nationalism stressed ancient Iran. The name “Iran” was requested internationally in 1935.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick courtyard houses; bread (nan), rice, kebabs and tea.

neighbours.value: The Russian Empire/USSR, the Ottoman Empire/Turkey, British India, Afghanistan and the Gulf states.

ideasReligions.value: Constitutionalism and nationalism from Europe. Khomeini’s revolutionary Islamism spread from 1979.
ideasReligions.source: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

colonisation.value: Never formally colonised, but heavily influenced by Russia and Britain (spheres of influence, 1907) and occupied in both World Wars.

riseSignals.value: Agha Mohammad Khan reunified Iran (1789–96). Reza Shah later built a centralised modern state (1925 onwards).

peakPeriod.value: The oil boom of the 1970s under Mohammad Reza Shah.

declineSignals.value: Territorial losses and foreign concessions (Qajar). Under the Pahlavis: authoritarian rule, uneven development, falling oil revenue (1977), and clerical and leftist opposition.

outcome.value: Revolution. The 1979 Iranian Revolution, led by Ayatollah Khomeini, ended the monarchy on 11 February 1979. The Islamic Republic was declared on 1 April 1979.

sources.value: Court chronicles, British and Russian archives, censuses (1956, 1966, 1976). Checked against Wikipedia (“Qajar Iran”, “Pahlavi Iran”) on 6 Nov 2026. See also Abrahamian (2008).

overallCertainty.value: Good for events. Assessments of the Pahlavi era (modernisation versus dictatorship) are debated. Second source: Wikidata’s Qajar item ends in 1925; this app combines Qajar and Pahlavi Iran (to 1979).
